old.exp: The board runs the scheme and issues the seal, which is why a Cape origin claim is auditable rather than merely asserted. SAWIS is a real organisation doing a different job, gathering the industry's statistics, and the Cape Winemakers Guild is a voluntary association of winemakers.

new.exp: The authority runs the scheme and issues the seal, which is why a Cape origin claim is auditable rather than merely asserted; it took the work over from the Wine and Spirit Board, the name older books give, on 1 August 2023. SAWIS is a real organisation doing a different job, gathering the industry's statistics, and the Cape Winemakers Guild is a voluntary association of winemakers.

applied.old: Every certified wine is chemically analysed and tasted blind by the Wine and Spirit Board's panels, and a faulty wine fails whatever its paperwork says. The seal is therefore a statement about the liquid as well as the ledger, which is not true of every origin system in the world.
applied.new: Every certified wine is chemically analysed and tasted blind by the panels of the Wine Certification Authority (the Wine and Spirit Board until 2023), and a faulty wine fails whatever its paperwork says. The seal is therefore a statement about the liquid as well as the ledger, which is not true of every origin system in the world.

applied.verified: one search: legislation.govt.nz gives the title Geographical Indications Registration Act 2006, the change made on 1 May 2024 by section 21 of the European Union Free Trade Agreement Legislation Amendment Act 2024, which widened the regime to other goods

old.ans: The Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Act
old.exp: The Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Act defines a name's boundary and gives its users legal standing to defend it, at home and in trade negotiations abroad, and that is all it does: no variety, yield or winemaking rule attaches to any New Zealand name. Registration is voluntary and paid for by the applying industry body, which is why the register filled up only once export agreements made the protection worth buying.

new.exp: Its title was the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Act until 1 May 2024, when an amendment for the trade agreement with the European Union opened it to other goods and shortened the name. It defines a name's boundary and gives its users legal standing to defend it, at home and in trade negotiations abroad, and that is all it does: no variety, yield or winemaking rule attaches to any New Zealand name. Registration is voluntary and paid for by the applying industry body, which is why the register filled up only once export agreements made the protection worth buying.

applied.note: The accept list is unchanged: it already took the new title and still takes the old one, so check-regression loses nothing (0 of 12,115 probes). The stem (passed 2006, in force 2017) is true of the Act under either title.
applied.source: Geographical Indications Registration Act 2006 as amended by the European Union Free Trade Agreement Legislation Amendment Act 2024, s 21 (legislation.govt.nz, act/public/2006/60); IPONZ, European Union Geographical Indications and changes to legislation

old.q: More than double a barrique in one cask, the 500-litre format lets Syrah producers buy oak's slow breathing without its vanilla shouting. Name the format.
old.exp: More than doubling the volume cuts the wood surface each litre of wine touches by roughly a quarter, so flavour and oxygen both arrive at a gentler pace and the fruit stays in front. Syrah cellars from the northern Rhone to the Barossa lean on the size for exactly that restraint, often buying it new where a new barrique would shout.

new.q: A third larger than the 225-litre barrique, the 300-litre cask on the Court's list of barrel sizes lets Syrah take oak's slow breathing with less of its vanilla. Name the format.
new.exp: The Court's guide puts the puncheon at 300 litres, between the barrique and the 600-litre demi-muid, and that is the figure its paper marks, though the trade stretches the name to the 450 to 500 litre casks of the Barossa and the Rhone. The extra volume trims the wood each litre of wine touches by about a tenth, so flavour and oxygen arrive at a gentler pace and the fruit stays in front, which is why Syrah cellars often buy the bigger cask new where a new barrique would shout.

applied.note: The one stem edit of this pass, made because the litre figure IS the tested fact and the Court's paper marks the puncheon at 300: a stem keyed Puncheon for 500 litres drills the figure the Certified paper marks wrong, which no explanation can undo. The stem pins the Court's list, so hogshead (the trade's usual 300 litre name) is not taken. Key and accept list unchanged. The surface claim is re-worked for the new volume ((225/300) to the power of one third is 0.91, about a tenth less wood per litre). The CMS fragment e-3i0uh0tm (largest size on the Court's list, keyed Foudre) asks a different rung of the same ladder, a different task. The module docstring's two puncheon notes follow the change. check-similarity r2_viticulture_winemaking: 0 flagged, max ratio 0.233, longest shared run 3.
applied.source: the Court's curriculum guide (CMS-A 8.2023), page 7, Fermentation Vessels Types, Barrel Sizes
